newsitem.title: USA: First Merchants report irregular financial statements.
newsitem.headline: First Merchants report irregular financial statements.

text.p: First Merchants Acceptance Corp., a used automobile financer, said Wednesday it has found irregularities involving unauthorised entries in its financial records and had fired its president and other executives.
The lender, which specialises in consumers with limited access to traditional credit, said it fired its President and Chief Executive Officer Mitchell Kahn.
It also said it fired Thomas Ehm, vice president and chief information officer and formerly chief financial officer, Paul Van Eyl, vice president for strategic planning, and another employee.
Attempts to reach the fired officers were unsuccesful.

An investigation ordered by the board of directors is being conducted by Norman Smagley, the newly named senior vice president and chief financial officer, together with the company's outside counsel and independent auditors.
The Deerfield, Ill.-based company said it expects to restate 1996 earnings, initially reported at $10.5 million, or $1.56 a share, but expects the earnings for the year will be at least $1 a share.

The company also said its first quarter results will be delayed, but that it anticipates a loss of $1.60 to $2 a share because of a significant increase in the provision for credit losses reflecting changes in management's estimates of projected required reserves.

Smagley said in a news release that the irregularities resulted in the company being out of compliance with certain covenants under its financing arrangements. But all payments due under such arrangements have been made on a timely basis and the company is in discussion with its leaders and the credit enhancer of its securitizations.
The restated results are expected in May, the company said.
Two directors, William Plamondon and Richard Uhl, will serve as co-chief executive officers while a search is conducted for a new chief executive.

The problems at First Merchants come less than three months after Lake Forest, Ill.-based Mercury Finance said it would have to restate earnings for the last four years, cutting profits by about $90 million, because of what it said were accounting descrepencises.

Since then, Mercury has defaulted on millions of dollars in debt, come under an FBI investigation and has been named a defendant in more than half a dozen lawsuits surrounding the misstated earnings. The company also lost more than $2 billion in market capitalisation when the stock plunged following its cut earnings.
But the company has so far avoid the bankruptcy filing many analysts had predicted and has secured short-term financing.
